title: The Tide Ledger
subtitle: A serial for Kullangal Vaarte
blurb: A junior reporter in Mangaluru is handed a ledger and a warning. Original fiction, written for this paper: all people and companies in it are invented.
bible:
SERIAL: 'The Tide Ledger', a cosy-but-tense coastal mystery. ORIGINAL FICTION written for Kullangal Vaarte. All characters, companies and events are invented; never use real people or real companies.
SETTING: Mangaluru (old port, Bunder, Hampankatta), Malpe harbour (Udupi), Kundapura. Monsoon turning to post-monsoon October.
CAST: (also introduced in episodes 1-14: Tejas Shenoy, 24, large kind newspaper photographer who goes everywhere with Ira; Sharada, a fishwife at Malpe who knows where the diesel goes; Sheshappa, the Courier's old peon, loyal; Ganesh, the Kundapura stationer with the scanner; Mrs D'Souza, Ira's landlady; Prabhakar, Hegde's man in the white shirt; Sultan, Nirmala's black dog; Ira's mother, who keeps proposing a chartered accountant from Udupi.) Ira Rao (26, junior reporter, The Coastal Courier, sharp, impatient, gets seasick). Anthony Pinto (68, retired clerk of the Sasi Fishermen's Cooperative, gave her the ledger, then vanished). Deepak Nayak (30, Sub-Inspector, Ira's college friend, careful, funny). Leela Kamath (58, editor, cautious, secretly proud of Ira). Yusuf Beary (45, boat mechanic and source, knows every engine sound). Ramachandra 'R.K.' Hegde (60s, chairman of Sea Crest Marine Pvt Ltd and president of the cooperative, charming, generous, dangerous). Nirmala (Pinto's sister in Kundapura).
CORE MYSTERY: The ledger shows payments for 'ice and diesel' to Sea Crest Marine for 114 boats. Boat 114 and many others do not exist. Subsidised diesel meant for fishermen is being diverted and sold. Pinto kept the true record and hid it.
TONE AND LENGTH: a proper serial for grown-up readers, in the manner of a newspaper novel. Each episode is 850 to 1,100 words in 8 to 16 full paragraphs (long flowing paragraphs with dialogue run into them, not one-line stanzas), with one or two scene breaks (a paragraph that is exactly ***). Sensory coast detail (rain, diesel, fish, chai, Tulu and Konkani words), humour, a real sense of place, and an ending hook. Plain English, no gore, no crime tutorials.
EPISODES SO FAR: 1-14 written (Wed to Mon). Pinto kept TWO ledgers: the clean summary he gave Ira, and an older original book with signatures that he hid and says also incriminates him. Three copies of the scanned summary exist (Ira's shoe, a post to Mrs Kamath, Deepak's wallet). Deepak's senior officer already knew he was in Kundapura (a leak inside the police). Ep14 ends on Monday evening: Hegde and a lawyer have served the Courier with a court injunction against publishing; Mrs Kamath tells everyone to leave the office except Ira.
NEXT ARC (write episodes 15 onward in this order, one per day, adjusting if needed): 15 The injunction fight: Mrs Kamath is tempted to fold; Ira finds the injunction covers only 'unverified claims'. 16 Ira and Deepak trace the boat registrations to a clerk at the Fisheries office, Suma. 17 Suma refuses, then leaves a locker key. 18 The locker: a second, older ledger showing Pinto helped set up the scheme years ago (his secret). 19 Ira confronts Pinto in Kundapura; he explains he was pressured, kept records as insurance. 20 A cyclone warning; harbour empties; Hegde offers Pinto safety in exchange for the ledger. 21 Yusuf's workshop is set on fire; he is fine, angry. 22 Deepak's senior officer transfers him; he chooses to help off the books. 23 Ira gets a fisherman's union leader, Kalappa, to speak on record. 24 Storm night: the three copies of the ledger; one lost to water, one to Hegde's man, one survives with Ira. 25 Chase through the flooded Bunder lanes by auto-rickshaw. 26 The story runs on the front page after all the injunction is lifted by a judge who reads the raw ledger. 27 Raid on the ice plant and the Sea Crest office. 28 Hegde's charm cracks; he tries to bribe Ira with a Bengaluru job. 29 Cooperative election: Kalappa wins. Pinto testifies. 30 Ending: Ira turns down Bengaluru, chooses to stay, and gets seasick on her first ride with the fishermen. Then start a NEW cosy case with the same cast.

episodes.title: The Man with the Wet Umbrella
text: The monsoon had been sulking over Mangaluru for nine days, and by six o’clock that Wednesday evening the newsroom of The Coastal Courier smelled of wet paper, stale tea and the particular damp of a building that has never once been properly dry. Ira Rao sat at the desk nearest the window, typing up a story about a pothole on the road to Kodialbail that had swallowed an auto-rickshaw whole, and she was thinking, with some bitterness, that this was probably the most exciting thing that would happen to her all week. She was twenty-six. She had been at the paper for eleven months. In that time she had covered two ribbon-cuttings, a goat that had walked into a bank, and the long, slow, unresolved quarrel over who owned the parking space outside the Hampankatta fruit market. Her editor said she had a nose for a story. Ira privately felt the nose had so far found only the goat.

The door at the far end opened, and a man came in with an umbrella that had clearly lost its argument with the wind. Two of its ribs poked out like the bones of a small, tired bird. Water ran off his shirt and trousers and made a little lake on the floor around his chappals, and the peon, Sheshappa, who had been about to say something about wet floors, took one look at the man’s face and said nothing at all. He was perhaps sixty-eight, thin, with white hair combed flat in the careful way of a man who had once worked in an office and still dressed for it. He stood at the doorway and looked around the room slowly, the way a person looks around a bus station, checking every face. Then he looked at Ira, and his shoulders came down a fraction, as though he had found what he had come for.
“Miss Rao?” he said. “Ira Rao? You wrote about the diesel queue at Malpe.”
“Three months ago,” said Ira. She was surprised to find that she had stood up. “Nobody read it.”

“I read it. I cut it out and kept it.” He crossed the room, leaving wet footprints, and set a plastic bag on her desk. Inside, wrapped twice in newspaper, was a ledger with a cloth cover gone soft at the corners, the sort of bound accounts book that nobody had bought in a stationery shop for twenty years. “My name is Anthony Pinto. I was a clerk at the Sasi Fishermen’s Cooperative for thirty-one years. I retired two winters ago. You will not find my name in anything, Miss Rao, because clerks’ names are never in anything. That is the whole point of a clerk.”
Ira put a hand on the plastic bag but did not open it. “Mr Pinto, what is this?”

“It is the truth,” said Mr Pinto, “written in blue ink, in my own hand, over three years. It is not a pleasant truth and I have not been brave about it. I should have brought it a year ago. I have been sitting in my house for a year listening to the rain and telling myself that someone else would notice.” He swallowed. His throat moved like a boy’s. “Do not read it here. Do not read it in this building. Take it home, and read it somewhere the sea cannot hear.”
There was a short silence in which the ceiling fan ticked and somewhere in the next room a telephone rang and was ignored. Ira said, carefully, “That is a strange thing to say.”

“I know.” He tried to smile and did not quite manage it. “I am a strange old man. My sister says so. Good evening, Miss Rao. Thank you for writing about the queue.” He took up his broken umbrella, nodded gravely to Sheshappa, who nodded back as if they were two diplomats, and went out through the same door, leaving the lake behind him. Through the window, Ira watched him go down the stairs and out into the street, where the rain closed over him like water over a stone.

She did not read it in the newsroom. She did not, in fact, so much as open the plastic bag until she had finished the pothole story, filed it, cleared her desk, said goodnight to the sub-editors, and walked the long way round to the bus stop with the bag held against her ribs under her raincoat as though it were an injured animal. The bus to Kodialbail was full of wet umbrellas and the smell of frying onions from the roadside stalls, and at the Hampankatta signal it stopped for so long that the conductor got down and bought a packet of banana chips. Ira stood holding the rail and looked at the faces around her: a schoolgirl asleep on her mother’s shoulder, two men arguing in Tulu about a cricket match, a woman with a basket of jasmine garlands wrapped in banana leaf, the scent of them rising warm and sweet through the diesel and rain. It struck her that every one of these people had a ledger of some kind at home, in a drawer, in a trunk, in the back of their head, and that most of them would never hand it to a stranger on a wet Wednesday.

Her phone buzzed. It was her mother, which meant it would be about marriage. Ira let it ring out. She would call back after dinner and listen to a description of a very suitable boy, a chartered accountant from Udupi with a flat and a nice nature, and she would say, as she always did, that she was busy, and her mother would say that nobody was too busy for happiness. It was a conversation she could have recited in her sleep. For the first time in months she found that she did not mind having a reason to postpone it.

The bus lurched forward at last. Ira closed her eyes and held the bag a little tighter, and tried, without much success, to remember what kind of man puts a newspaper cutting about a diesel queue in his pocket and keeps it for three months.

episodes.title: Column Seven
episodes.recap: Ira Rao is at her desk in a Mangaluru newsroom when a retired clerk, soaked by the monsoon, hands her a ledger and a warning. She takes it home.
text: Ira’s flat was on the first floor of an old house in Kodialbail, above a tailor’s shop whose sewing machines went quiet at eight every night and began again, with a sound like a very small and very determined train, at half past eight the next morning. It had two rooms and a balcony that held a bucket and a bicycle. The landlady, Mrs D’Souza, lived downstairs and had views on everything from Ira’s hours to the state of the nation, but she also left a steel tiffin of rice and fish curry on the stairs on Wednesdays without ever mentioning it, which Ira understood to be love.

She ate the curry standing at the counter, because she was too restless to sit. Then she made a glass of ginger tea, spread an old bedsheet over the table for no reason she could name except that it seemed wrong to open the thing on a bare surface, and finally, with the rain drumming on the tin roof of the verandah below, she opened the ledger.

It was a plain accounts book, ruled in faded red, filled with entries in a small, upright, extraordinarily careful hand: dates, boat numbers, quantities of diesel, quantities of ice, the cost of nets mended and engines repaired. Page after page of it, thirty-one years’ worth of ordinary arithmetic, in the blue ink of someone who believed that a number written clearly could not be argued with. Ira turned the pages for a quarter of an hour and felt her eyes begin to slide. Anyone who has ever tried to read an accounts book for pleasure will understand. She almost closed it. She actually had her hand on the cover when she noticed that the entries on the right-hand pages had begun to change.

It was subtle. The handwriting was the same, but in the last three years of entries the columns had grown a seventh, headed in neat capitals ICE AND DIESEL, SEA CREST MARINE. The payments in column seven were not like the others. They were regular, they were large, and they were made to the same company, month after month, for boat after boat after boat. She counted. In March alone, the cooperative had paid Sea Crest Marine for ice and diesel for ninety-four boats. In April it was ninety-eight. By the time the pages reached the third winter it was a hundred and fourteen.

Ira, who was not good at sums but was very good at being suspicious of them, went and found a pencil and a page of rough paper and began to work. The Sasi Fishermen’s Cooperative, she knew from her own diesel-queue story, represented about sixty working boats. She had interviewed the secretary. She had counted the boats in the harbour with her own eyes, standing on the jetty in a drizzle, with a photographer who had kept complaining about his lens. Sixty boats. Not a hundred and fourteen. She added the page twice, and the second time more slowly, with her finger running down the column, and the total did not change. It was not a clerical slip. It was a number that someone had meant.

She might have talked herself out of it even then, because she was a reasonable person and reasonable people look for reasonable explanations. Perhaps the cooperative supplied boats from other harbours. Perhaps ice and diesel were bought in bulk for the whole coast. But at the bottom of that last page, in the thin margin beside the final total, there was a line in pencil, so faint that she had to tilt the lamp to catch it. It was the same small, upright hand, but pressed so lightly it looked like a thing written by someone who wanted it to be found and did not want it to be seen.
Boat 114 does not exist.

Ira sat very still. Outside, a scooter went through the puddle at the corner with a long sigh. Downstairs the tailor’s cat knocked something off a shelf and was shouted at in Konkani. The lamp hummed. She thought of the old man on the newsroom floor with his broken umbrella, saying read it where the sea cannot hear, and she thought, for the first time, that perhaps he had not been strange at all. Perhaps he had simply been afraid in the ordinary, well-informed way of someone who knows exactly how much a number is worth.

She took out her phone and photographed the page, then the one before it, then every page with a seventh column, working carefully, because the light was bad and her hands were not entirely steady. When she had finished it was after midnight and the rain had thinned to a whisper. She wrote three words at the top of a clean sheet, BOAT 114, and underlined them twice. Then she sat and watched the sheet as though it might reply.

At a quarter to one, she called her mother back. It was a ridiculous time, and her mother answered on the first ring, alarmed, and Ira said, “Amma, I’m fine. I only wanted to say, tell me about the chartered accountant,” and heard her mother go silent with astonishment, and then begin, slowly and with enormous care, to describe him, as though Ira were a deer that might bolt. It was, Ira found, a surprisingly comforting thing to listen to. A suitable boy, a flat in Udupi, a nice nature. She let her mother’s voice run on, warm and ordinary, and looked at the ledger on the table, which was neither.

episodes.title: Boat 114
episodes.recap: At home, Ira reads the ledger and finds a column of payments for ice and diesel to Sea Crest Marine, for 114 boats, and a pencilled note in the margin: Boat 114 does not exist.
text: The Fisheries office at the old port opened at ten, and Ira was on its steps by a quarter to, in a clean salwar and her most responsible expression, carrying a folder, a smile and a lie. The lie was that she was writing a feature on traditional boat numbering for the Sunday supplement. It was a perfectly good lie, in that nobody in the history of the Sunday supplement had ever checked it, but she did not enjoy telling it. She had been brought up by a mother who believed that a lie, even a small and useful one, left a smell in the house.

The old port, which everyone in Mangaluru called the Bunder, was at its most itself on a wet morning. The estuary was the colour of strong tea. Cargo boats sat low in the water with tarpaulins lashed down, and along the quay the porters in their red shirts and checked lungis were rolling barrels with the unhurried confidence of men who had done it every working day of their lives. There was a smell of fish, diesel, wet rope and the sweet rot of mangoes from a stall that should have been closed. Gulls stood on the bollards with the expressions of landlords. Ira climbed the stone steps of the Fisheries building, a colonial thing with a verandah and a sagging nameboard, and found the registration counter behind a wooden barrier at the end of a long, dim corridor lined with files tied in red cloth.

The clerk on duty was thin, with a pen in each shirt pocket and a calendar behind him that showed, unaccountably, a smiling fish in a bow tie. He listened to her story about the Sunday supplement with the polite blankness of a man who had heard many stories. Then he pulled a heavy register towards him, licked his thumb and began to turn the pages.

“One-fourteen,” he said, after a while. “Hmm.” He turned back. He turned forward again. He turned the whole register over, which is not a thing that helps, and looked at the spine, which also did not help. “It is not here, Madam. The numbers go up to one hundred and six. Then they stop. And then they start again at two hundred.”
“What happened to the numbers in between?”

He looked at her, and then at the door, and then at the calendar fish. His whole body seemed to decide, in the space of a second, to become deaf. “You will have to ask the cooperative,” he said, in the voice of a man reading aloud from a sign. “We only keep the register, Madam. What goes in it is not our concern.” He closed the book with some finality. “Would you like some tea?”

She declined the tea, thanked him, and went back down the stone steps feeling, for the first time, the particular cold sensation that comes when a small question turns out to have a large answer behind it. The rain had begun again, thin and fine. She stood under the verandah and looked at the boats on the water and wondered how many of them were numbered honestly.

Yusuf Beary’s boat yard was behind the fish market, down a lane so narrow that two people carrying anything wider than a bucket had to negotiate. It was a long, low shed open at one end to the water, with hulls propped on timber cradles in various stages of undress, and a smell of paint thinner and sawdust and hot metal. Yusuf was a mechanic of about forty-five who, it was said, could tell the age of a boat from the sound of its engine and the secrets of its owner from the way the owner refused to talk about it. Ira had met him once, on the diesel-queue story, when he had given her a glass of black tea and a better quote than the cooperative secretary. When she arrived he was lying under a hull on a wooden trolley, and only his feet, in cracked rubber sandals, were visible. They spoke first.
“Madam Reporter,” said the feet. “You are the only person in Mangaluru who comes to a boat yard in a clean dress.”
“I have a question about numbers.”
The feet stopped moving. After a pause, Yusuf slid out from under the hull, wiped his hands on a rag, and looked at her properly. His face was broad and lined and not unkind. “Which number?”
“One-fourteen.”

He said nothing for so long that she thought he had not heard. A gull walked along the roof of the shed. Down at the water, someone was hammering. Finally Yusuf folded the rag, very precisely, into a square. “Madam,” he said, “there are boats that go out at night with no lights. I fix the engines. I do not ask where they go. When a man has two daughters at college and a mother with a bad heart, he does not ask.” He glanced down the lane, left and right, as though water might have ears. “But if you ask about those boats again, ask quietly. Sound carries over water. And ask somewhere that is not here.

episodes.title: Missing
episodes.recap: At the harbour office a clerk goes suddenly deaf when Ira asks about Boat 114, and the boat mechanic Yusuf Beary warns her to ask quietly.
text: On Thursday morning Ira rang Mr Pinto’s number and got a polite recorded voice telling her that the person she was calling could not be reached. She tried again at noon from the newsroom, standing by the window with one finger in her other ear against the clatter of the printers, and again at four, and by then she had stopped pretending that she was only being thorough. She went back to her desk and wrote the heading of a story she could not write, The Missing Clerk, and then deleted it, because a missing person is a thing the police report and the family reports, and she had no right to either. At a quarter past five she gave up, slung her bag over her shoulder and took the bus to Bolar.

The address on the old cooperative card in the ledger’s plastic bag led, after two wrong turns and a conversation with a man selling coconuts, to a small blue house at the end of a lane. It had a tulsi plant in a cement pot on the step, a jasmine creeper strangling the gate, and a padlock the size of a fist on the front door. The padlock was not new, but it was clean. Someone had cleaned it that week, the way people clean a thing they intend to leave. Ira stood at the gate with the rain running off the end of her umbrella and found, to her annoyance, that her heart was going faster than the walk justified.
“He is not here, beta.”

The voice came from the next verandah, where an old woman in a faded green nightie and a woollen cap, in spite of the heat, sat on a plastic chair with a bowl of beans on her lap. She was stringing them into a steel plate without looking, the way people do a thing they have done ten thousand times, and watching Ira with frank, interested, entirely unembarrassed eyes.
“When did he leave?” said Ira.

“Yesterday, before sunrise. I was up for my knees. I saw him from the window. He had a small cloth bag and no umbrella.” The old woman pursed her lips. “That man has carried an umbrella every day for thirty years, rain or sun. He carried it to the temple. He carried it to the funeral of his wife. When I saw him go without it I thought, something is wrong. Then I thought, no, it is a mercy, God has finally made him forget it.” She dropped a bean into the plate. “But he did not forget. He left it in the rack. It is still there. Look, through the window.”

Ira looked. In the dim hall, hung neatly on a hook as though it had been placed there by someone saying goodbye, was the other umbrella, the good one, with a bamboo handle. The one that had come to the newsroom must have been the old one, the one he did not mind losing.
“Did anyone come to see him?” said Ira.

The old woman’s hands paused. She looked, for a moment, less like a nosy neighbour and more like a person remembering something she had been unwilling to know. “Two young men on a scooter, last week. Thursday, perhaps. They did not knock. They stood at the gate and looked at the house for a long time. One of them took a photograph with his phone. Then they went away. The other one wore a white shirt.” She dropped another bean. “Nobody wears a white shirt in this lane in the monsoon, beta. Not unless he is going to a wedding or a funeral.”

Ira thanked her, because it was the only thing she could think of to do, and stood for a while in the lane while the streetlight at the corner flickered on and moths began to throw themselves at it. The ledger was heavy in her bag. She felt, suddenly and unpleasantly, like someone carrying an egg through a crowd. Every scooter that passed seemed to slow a little. Every man in a doorway seemed to be looking in her direction. It was ridiculous, she told herself, and she knew from experience that it did not matter whether a feeling was ridiculous; it only mattered whether it was right.

She sat down on the low wall of a closed pharmacy and took out her phone and scrolled, with a small bitter reluctance, to a name she had not used since her last year at college. Deepak Nayak. They had sat together in Introduction to Journalism, he in the back row drawing cartoons of the professor, she in the front row taking notes. Then he had unexpectedly cleared the police sub-inspector exam, to the astonishment of everyone including, she suspected, himself, and she had gone to the Courier, and they had stayed friends in the way of people who exchange festival greetings and a few jokes a year. His last message to her was a photograph of a very sad samosa, captioned: Station canteen. Please send help.
She looked at the photograph for a moment. Then she did the thing that she had spent twenty-six years learning not to do, which was to ask for help before she knew exactly what she was asking for.

She pressed call. It rang four times. She nearly hung up, with the relief of a person who has been spared a decision, and then a tired, familiar voice said, “Ira Rao. Are you getting married? Because if you are, I am busy that day.”
“No,” said Ira. “Deepak, I think someone has gone missing. And I think I am carrying the reason.”

There was a long pause on the line. Somewhere behind him a door banged and a man laughed. When Deepak spoke again, his voice had changed. It was lower and slower, and it had lost all its jokes. “Where are you?” he said. “Do not move. Do not tell me anything on the phone. I will meet you at the tea stall by the police lines at eight. And Ira. Take a different road home.”

episodes.title: The Sub-Inspector
episodes.recap: Mr Pinto has vanished from his house in Bolar, leaving his good umbrella behind, and a neighbour remembers two men on a scooter, one in a white shirt. Ira rings her old college friend, Sub-Inspector Deepak Nayak.
text: They met at the tea stall opposite the police lines because Deepak said that police stations had ears, and that walls, in his experience, repeated things. It was a tin shed with a smoky stove, a glass case of stale biscuits and three plastic stools, run by an old man in a vest who made tea in an aluminium pot so blackened with use that it looked like a piece of the night itself. Rain dripped from the tin roof onto the road in a bead curtain. Deepak was already there, sitting very straight on a stool that was too low for him, in plain clothes, with an expression of studied cheerfulness that did not fool her for a second.

He was thinner than she remembered. His moustache, which had been a joke at college, a thin, ironical line, was now a decision. He had the look of a man who has spent a year learning exactly how little can be done about most things. But when she sat down on the next stool and put the plastic bag on her knees and said, “Don’t laugh,” he looked at her face and his own face went still, and she remembered why she had called him.

“A missing person,” he said at last, stirring sugar into his tea. “Adult male, retired, left of his own free will with a bag. Ira, do you know how many of those I have on my desk? I have eleven. Four of them are husbands who have gone to Dubai without telling their wives. Two are grandfathers who got on the wrong bus. I do not even have a form for a man who leaves his umbrella at home.”
“I know how many of them had a visit from two men on a scooter,” said Ira, “and one of them in a white shirt.”

The spoon stopped. He didn’t look up. She told him everything, in order, in a low voice, while the old man at the stove pretended to arrange his biscuits: the ledger, the seven columns, the three years of sums that could not be sums, the margin in pencil, the clerk at the registry with his tidy deafness, Yusuf Beary’s feet and the lane with ears. She did not tell him about the old man’s face in the newsroom doorway, because that was not evidence, and also because it was the part she kept returning to. When she finished, the tea in front of her had grown a skin and the rain had settled into a long steady drum on the roof.
Deepak looked at the road for what felt like a full minute. “Sea Crest Marine,” he said finally. “Do you know who owns it?”
“No.”

“R K Hegde.” He said it quietly, as one says the name of a temple god. “The Chairman. He is also the president of the cooperative. He opened the new wing of the hospital in Kunjibettu. He paid for the school bus in my village for six years, Ira. My mother has his photograph in the puja room, next to Ganesha, because of what he did when my uncle was ill. He sits on four trusts and two temple committees. If you stood on the Bunder and asked a hundred people who the best man in Mangaluru is, I would say eighty would name him.”
“That doesn’t make him honest.”

“It doesn’t make him dishonest either.” He rubbed his face with both hands. When they came down, he looked, for a moment, almost like the boy who had drawn cartoons in the back row. Then he took out a small black notebook that was very clearly not police property, flipped to a clean page and wrote something on it. “I will make one call,” he said. “Unofficial. If anyone ever asks, we discussed cricket. Do you understand me? You and I talked about cricket, and I think India’s middle order is a disgrace.”

He was gone for twenty-two minutes. Ira spent them watching the rain and the lights of the police lines, a long yellow building with a flag drooping from a pole, and wondering whether this was how it began, the thing that people later called the turning point in a story: not with a bang, or a speech, but with a woman on a plastic stool and a cup of cold tea and a friend walking away across a wet road with his phone to his ear. When he came back he sat down slowly, as though the stool had become fragile, and put the phone face down on his knee.

“Mr Pinto took the six-fifteen bus to Udupi on Wednesday morning,” he said. “A conductor on the route remembers him because he paid the exact fare, in coins, and asked the conductor to tell him when they reached Malpe junction. He did not get off at Udupi. He got off at Malpe.” He turned the phone over, looked at it, and turned it back. “And his phone, which has been off since yesterday, woke up once, for four minutes, at half past eleven last night. A tower near Malpe harbour.”
“He is hiding,” said Ira. “Or someone is hiding him.”

“Or someone has found him,” said Deepak, and then, seeing her face, added, much more gently, “I am only telling you the three things that are true. I don’t know which of them it is. Ira, I will tell you the fourth true thing, and it is the one that matters. If this ledger says what you think it says, you are carrying something heavy through a city where a great many people like the man who may not want you to carry it. You are very clever. You are also, if I may say so, a person who has never once taken a different road home when told to.”

She said nothing. The rain pattered on. The old man at the stove took the skin off her cold tea with a spoon, set a fresh glass in front of her without a word, and went back to his biscuits. She drank it. It was very hot and very sweet and exactly what she needed.
“I am going to Malpe,” she said. “At dawn. Before the boats go out.”
Deepak put his head in his hands. “Of course you are,” he said, to the road, to the rain, to the long yellow building with its drooping flag. “Of course you are.”

episodes.title: Malpe at Dawn
episodes.recap: Over tea by the police lines, Deepak agrees to make one unofficial call. Mr Pinto took a bus to Malpe, and his phone woke up once near the harbour. Ira decides to go at dawn.
text: Nobody had warned Ira that a fishing harbour at five in the morning is the loudest place in the world. She had imagined something misty and still, with silhouettes of men and nets against a pale sky, something out of a school textbook. What she got, stepping off the first Udupi bus into a darkness that smelled of salt and diesel and drying fish, was a noise like a stadium: engines coughing into life one after another, men shouting to men sixty feet away across the water, a radio playing a Kannada film song at full volume, gulls screaming at one another about property rights, and somewhere in the middle of it all a man selling tea and shouting about it, as though tea were a political cause.

Malpe harbour was a long concrete basin crowded with boats, so many and so tightly packed that a determined person could have walked from one side to the other without touching water. They were painted blue and green and orange and white, each with a number on the bow and a name in letters that leaned into the wind: names of saints and gods and daughters and film stars. Women in bright saris and rubber boots were already at the auction shed with baskets on their heads, haggling over silver heaps of sardines and mackerel that gleamed like spilled coins under the hanging bulbs. A dog, who seemed to be in charge, picked its way among the baskets with the air of an inspector. Ira pulled her scarf up over her hair, put her phone away, and tried to look like a person who had every reason to be interested in ice.

It was a woman who spoke to her first. She was about fifty, heavy-set, with a basket of mackerel on her hip and a face as brown and creased as a good leather bag, and she looked at Ira’s clean shoes with an expression of enormous, tolerant amusement. “You are from the newspaper,” she said, in Kannada, not unkindly. “I know that walk. You write about us when the price goes up and forget us when it comes down.”
“I wrote about the diesel queue,” said Ira, a little stung. “In June.”

“Ah. That one.” The woman shifted her basket. “My name is Sharada. My husband’s boat has been stuck on the quota for three months. They say there is no subsidised diesel left. But I have seen the diesel go. Not here, not at the pump, in the dark, in barrels, on a lorry that does not say Fisheries on its side.” She spat, delicately, into the harbour. “You write that. Or don’t. It makes no difference to me. I only sell fish.” She turned, called something sharp to a boy with a trolley, and moved off through the crowd before Ira could ask her anything at all.

It took Ira twenty minutes of apparently aimless walking to notice the boat. She had gone to the far end of the harbour, where the berths were quieter and the boats sat a little lower in the water, and she was pretending to photograph the sunrise, which was breaking at last through the cloud in a long smear of pink and gold. She saw it because it was the only boat on the whole quay with no one on its deck. It sat a little too low in the water, laden with something heavy beneath its tarpaulin. Its name had been painted out with white paint, in a hurry, and the number on the bow too. Someone had given it one coat and then, presumably interrupted, not gone back for the second. Under the white, faint as a bruise on pale skin, she could read three digits.
One. One. Four.

Her heart did something enthusiastic and unhelpful. She lifted her phone, as casually as she could, and took a picture of the sunrise with the boat very slightly to one side of it. She took another with the zoom. She was moving closer, to the edge of the quay where a rusty bollard stood, to read the paint on the stern, when a voice behind her said, quite politely, “Madam.”

He stood at her elbow. She had not heard him come. He was not tall, but he had the sort of stillness that is more frightening than height, the kind that men acquire when they have been told what to do by people who are never present. He wore a clean white shirt with the sleeves rolled exactly twice, grey trousers, black leather shoes in a harbour where every other person was barefoot or in rubber. Nobody wore a white shirt at Malpe at five in the morning. Ira remembered, with a small cold shock, the old woman’s voice. Nobody wears a white shirt in the monsoon, beta, unless he is going to a wedding or a funeral.
“This area is for fishermen,” he said. “For your safety, Madam. The edge is slippery.”
“Of course,” said Ira. “I was just leaving.”
“There is a very good tea stall near the bus stand,” the man said, and smiled, and the smile did not touch any other part of his face. “You must try it before you go.”

She walked away at exactly the speed of someone who has nothing to hide, past the baskets and the shouting women and the dog who was still, presumably, in charge, and did not turn round. She had gone about thirty steps when she heard behind her, clear as a bell in the harbour noise, the small, flat, unmistakable click of a phone camera. It was the sound of a photograph being taken of the back of her head.

episodes.title: Mrs Kamath Says No
episodes.recap: At dawn in Malpe harbour a fishwife tells Ira the subsidised diesel is vanishing in the night. Ira spots a boat with its number painted over, 114, and a man in a white shirt takes her photograph.
text: Leela Kamath had run The Coastal Courier for eleven years, through two floods, one bus strike and a printing press that had once caught fire in the middle of a cricket special, and the staff said that the only thing in the building older than her glasses was the smell. She was fifty-eight, short and square in a cotton sari, with grey hair in a bun that looked as if it had been put on with a hammer. She did not shout. She had never needed to. She read copy with her glasses on the end of her nose and her eyebrows on holiday, and when she disapproved of a sentence the whole newsroom could feel it, like a drop in air pressure before a storm.

Ira stood in front of her desk with her notes in her hand. It was Friday morning. She had not slept more than three hours, and she had taken, on the way in, a path that led round the back of the building, past the bins, and through a service door, a precaution so absurd that she had not dared to mention it to anyone. In the glass-walled office the ceiling fan turned slowly. A framed front page from the 2009 floods hung on the wall behind Mrs Kamath’s head, the headline in letters three inches high: THE WATER DOES NOT CARE.
“A ledger,” said Mrs Kamath, when Ira had finished, “from a retired clerk who has disappeared. A margin note in pencil. A boat number visible under some white paint. And a man in a white shirt.”
“And a scooter,” said Ira.

“And a scooter.” Mrs Kamath took off her glasses and pinched the bridge of her nose. “Ira, I will tell you what I see, and you will not like it, and I would like you to listen to the end before you say anything. I see a very good beginning. I see the first two pages of a story that I would give a year of my life to print. And I see nothing that I could put in front of a lawyer.” She put the glasses back on. “Do you know who places a full-page advertisement with us every Tuesday?”
“No.”

“Neither do I. That is what worries me. I have not looked. I have been editing this paper for eleven years, and I am afraid I have formed the habit of not looking at the one column of the accounts that is always paid on time.” She leaned back. The chair creaked. “If I print what you have given me, Mr Hegde’s lawyers will stand on this desk. They will use words like defamation and malicious. And they will be right, because you have given me a hunch, a pencil mark and a photograph of a boat. I cannot hang a man on a hunch, Ira. Not even a good one.”

There was a long silence. Through the glass wall the newsroom hummed on without them: the clack of keyboards, a phone, the sub-editors’ low continual argument about the Oxford comma. Ira felt her face go hot, and then, strangely, cool. She had expected the refusal. What she had not expected was how reasonable it would sound.

“Get me a second source,” said Mrs Kamath, more gently. “Get me paper I can hold in my hand, with a signature on it or a stamp. Get me a person who is willing to say the same thing on the record. You have three days, until Monday evening, and I will give you every hour of the Courier’s time I can, and I will tell no one in this building what you are doing. If you come to me on Monday with nothing, we will put it away and go on with the pothole stories and you will not feel that you have failed. And if you come to me with what you hope to come with,” and here, for the first time, something that was almost a smile moved at the corner of her mouth, “then I shall want a very large font.”
“Thank you,” said Ira, and meant it, and found, absurdly, that she was close to tears.
“Ira.” She had turned to go. Mrs Kamath was looking down at the notes on her desk, and her voice was quite level. “The man in the white shirt at Malpe. Did he see your face?”
“Yes.”

“Then from now on you do not go anywhere alone. I mean it. You will take Tejas. He is a bad photographer and a very large boy, which in the circumstances is a recommendation. Tejas! Come here, and bring your camera, and do not look so pleased.”

A young man had appeared in the doorway as if summoned by a spell: twenty-four, six feet tall, built like an almirah, with a rumpled shirt, an expression of joyous apprehension and a camera bag over each shoulder. Tejas Shenoy had been at the Courier for a year, and had so far photographed three weddings, a coconut-tree accident and, to his permanent regret, the inside of a refrigerator for a feature on food safety. He looked from one woman to the other, plainly delighted by the prospect of being in on something.
“Where are we going?” he said.

“Nowhere yet,” said Mrs Kamath. “Sit down, Tejas. And Ira, one more thing.” She was looking at her now, over the glasses, and her face had changed, and Ira understood that she was looking at her as a mother might, if the mother were very practical and slightly afraid. “It was the kindest thing anyone ever did for me, when I started, that someone told me not to be brave alone. So I am telling you.”

episodes.title: The Chairman
episodes.recap: Editor Leela Kamath refuses to print a hunch, gives Ira until Monday evening to find a second source, and orders the photographer Tejas Shenoy to go everywhere with her.
text: The invitation came on thick cream paper in a cream envelope, delivered by hand on Saturday morning by a boy in a white uniform who stood in the newsroom doorway with the stiff dignity of a ceremonial guard. R K Hegde, Chairman, Sea Crest Marine Private Limited, requests the pleasure of Miss Ira Rao’s company at lunch at one o’clock today at his residence. A car will be sent. Ira read it twice, put it down on her desk and looked at it as one looks at a snake that has been delivered in a gift basket. Then she showed it to Tejas, who read it with his mouth slightly open and said, “Nobody has ever invited me to lunch on cream paper. I would be afraid.”
“I am afraid,” said Ira.
“Then why are you going?”

“Because if I refuse, he knows I know. And if I go, he doesn’t know how much.” She picked up the card and tucked it into her bag. “Also, Tejas, I would like to see what a person has in his house when he has everything.”

She went, with Deepak’s number on speed dial and her phone recording in the pocket of her kurta, and with the strange light, nervous feeling of a woman walking into an examination in a subject she had not quite studied. The car was a long grey Innova with a driver who never spoke. It took her through the old part of the city and up the hill towards Kadri, past the temple where the cows slept under the banyans, and turned in at a white gate that opened as they approached, as though the house had been watching the road. At the end of a gravel drive stood a big, low, whitewashed bungalow with a red-tiled roof, a long verandah and a lawn so green it looked rendered in paint. A peacock walked across it. Ira, who had seen peacocks in the wild, found it hard to believe the peacock had not been arranged.

Mr Hegde met her on the verandah himself. He was a broad, silver-haired man of about sixty-five, in a plain white shirt and mundu, with a gentle, rumbling voice and a laugh that made people feel they had just said something very clever. He took both her hands in his, said, “Miss Rao! How kind. You have come in the rain,” and led her through a cool, dim hallway lined with framed photographs: Mr Hegde with a chief minister, Mr Hegde with a cricketer, Mr Hegde cutting a ribbon at a hospital, Mr Hegde presenting a giant cheque to a school. The office he showed her into had a view across the whole estuary, a teak desk the size of a small boat, and, along one wall, a fish tank so large and so luminous that for a moment she thought it was a window onto the sea itself. Fish slid through it, silver and blue and slow.

He served her lunch himself, from a side table, with the unforced courtesy of a man who has hosted many guests and genuinely enjoys it: sukka with fresh coconut, neer dosa as thin as muslin, fried anjal, a bowl of the best solkadi she had ever tasted, a glass of buttermilk in which a single curry leaf floated. He asked whether she liked her tea with cardamom. He asked after her mother. It was, she realised, the sort of lunch that one gives to a person one wishes to remember kindly.

“You are the young lady who wrote about our diesel queues,” he said, sitting down across from her, tearing a dosa with his fingers. “A good piece. Fair. A little too gentle on the cooperative, if I may say so, but fair. I have been trying to fix that queue for ten years, Miss Rao. The government sends the quota. The pumps ration it. Everyone blames the middleman, and the middleman is generally a poor man with a lorry and a family. It is a very old coast, and an old coast has very old problems.” He smiled. “You are young. I am glad that someone young is looking.”
“You are the president of the cooperative,” said Ira.
“And its oldest friend.” He wiped his fingers. “I understand you have been asking about boat numbers. Ask me. I can save you a great deal of walking.”

For a moment she very nearly liked him. That was the dangerous thing about it. He was so easy, so warm, so entirely without the nervousness she had expected. She could see why the whole city loved him. She could see why Deepak’s mother kept his photograph beside Ganesha. She had opened her mouth to ask the careful question she had prepared, in three versions, on the car ride, when her eye fell on the teak desk and the small silver frame that stood at its corner.

It was a photograph of a boat. A very old photograph, black and white, with a man’s arm in the corner and the sea behind. The boat was drawn up on a beach with her nets heaped in the bows, and on her prow there had once been a number. Someone had removed it. Not by cutting, nor by tearing. Whoever had owned the photograph had, at some time, carefully painted out the number with correction fluid, so that the boat sat on the beach with a small white patch on its face like a patient with a plaster over one eye.
“You have a lovely office,” said Ira, as steadily as she could.
“And you have a very steady voice,” said Mr Hegde, still smiling, still gentle, and picked up his buttermilk. “You should be careful with it, Miss Rao. A voice like that can carry a very long way.”

episodes.title: A Message in the Margin
episodes.recap: R K Hegde, chairman of Sea Crest Marine, invites Ira to lunch, charms her completely and then warns her, gently. On his desk is a photograph of a boat whose number has been painted out.
text: She had been reading the ledger like a story, from the front to the back, and by Saturday night she had read it so many times that the figures had stopped meaning anything and had become a kind of music. Tejas, who had come up to her flat with a bag of hot onion pakoras and had been sitting on the floor against the wall with his long legs folded like a deckchair, said that it was the wrong way to read an accounts book. “I did a month in a bank,” he said, with a pakora halfway to his mouth, “before they found out about my handwriting. You know what the old clerks used to say? They said an honest man writes at the front of a ledger, and a frightened man writes at the back.”
“Where did you hear that?”
“I didn’t. I made it up. But it sounds true, doesn’t it?” He grinned. “Try the back.”

It was after ten. The rain had thinned to a silvery whisper against the window and the tailor’s machines downstairs had been quiet for hours. Forty kilometres away her mother, who had been told on the phone that her daughter was “working late with a colleague,” was no doubt composing a very long and hopeful message about a certain chartered accountant from Udupi. Ira turned the ledger over on the table, so that its last page lay face-up and its cover lay open like a hand. She had never looked at the back. Nobody ever looks at the back.

There was nothing in the last column, nor on the inside of the cover. But on the thick cardboard flap, where the cloth had lifted a little at the corner, someone had written, in pencil, and then carefully tried to rub it out. She held the page up to the lamp and tilted it, and the graphite caught the light in tiny silver ridges, like frost on a window. Three words, a number, and a fourth word.
“Ice plant,” she read aloud. “Back shed. Nine.”
Tejas stopped chewing. “Nine what? Nine o’clock? Nine barrels? Nine of something?”

“I don’t know.” She turned the board slightly and the light moved. Below that, in a smaller hand, as though the writer had thought better of it and then not been able to resist, were two more lines. She read them twice before she trusted herself. “They think I burned the old book. I did not.”

Neither of them said anything for a while. A moth bumped against the lampshade. Outside, an auto-rickshaw went by with its radio on, a Kannada song of the kind that is sad and cheerful at the same time, and faded away down the road. It was Tejas who spoke first, quietly, and for the first time since she had known him he did not sound pleased.
“There is another ledger.”

“An older one.” Ira sat back. “Mr Pinto kept two. The one that came to me is the clean copy, the one with everything neatly summarised so that someone could read it in a night. The other is the real one: the original, with every date and every signature and every stamp. And someone thought they had destroyed it.” She put her hand flat on the cover. “That is what the men on the scooter wanted. Not this. This is only the summary. They want the book that says who signed.”
“And he is still alive enough,” said Tejas slowly, “to lie about it.”
“Yes.”

She rang Deepak, who answered on the sixth ring in a voice thick with sleep and said, in the tone of a man who had been given a puzzle by a cat, “Cricket. We are talking about cricket.” She read him the note. There was a long silence, and then the sound of him sitting up in bed, “The ice plant is the old Sasi plant on the lane behind the cold-storage yard,” he said. “It was shut after the last monsoon. Notice on the gate says under renovation. In four months I have not seen one workman go in. Tell me you are not going to say what I think you are going to say.”
“Tomorrow night,” said Ira. “At nine.”

“I knew it,” said Deepak, to the ceiling, with deep sorrow. “I knew it. I am coming with you. Do not say a word, I am coming, and I am wearing dark clothes, and if anyone asks, we are looking for a lost cat. Tejas, are you there? You will wait at the end of the lane with the motorbike, and you will keep your phone in your hand, and if you see a car, you ring Ira. If you see a second car, you ring me. If you see a third car, you ring the police station, and then you ride away very fast and you do not stop.”
“Yes, sir,” said Tejas, with the unfeigned rapture of a man who has been given a role in a film.

When they had gone, she sat for a long time at the table with the ledger open under the lamp and the thin pencilled words glimmering on the cardboard. They think I burned the old book. I did not. It struck her, as she turned off the light, that of all the sentences in all the ledgers in the world, that was the one that a clerk would find hardest to write: not I was afraid, not I was wrong, but I did not. The simplest sentence a man can say, and the only one that might get him killed.

episodes.title: The Ice Plant
episodes.recap: Ira finds a hidden pencil note on the back of the ledger: Ice plant. Back shed. Nine. Under it: They think I burned the old book. I did not.
text: The Sasi ice plant stood at the end of a lane that smelled of old fish and new ambition. It was a tall, windowless building of grey concrete, stained black down the walls by years of leaking pipes, with a pair of iron gates chained shut and a faded board that said UNDER RENOVATION in letters that no longer seemed to expect to be believed. Behind it stretched the cold-storage yards, rows of dark sheds and rusting lorries, and beyond them the black flat shine of the estuary, with the lights of the harbour hanging in the wet air like lamps on a ceiling. It was five minutes to nine on Sunday night, and it was not raining, which in the monsoon is a sort of warning in itself.
“Explain to me again,” whispered Deepak, from the shadow of a parked lorry, “why this is not a bad idea.”
“Because it is a good idea that looks bad,” whispered Ira.

“I am a police officer. Bad ideas are my whole profession.” He was wearing a black T-shirt, black jeans, and a cap pulled low, and he looked, she thought, exactly like a man who has gone to a fancy dress party as a burglar. “I have written the word ‘recce’ on a form for this. In my own hand. If I fall off a roof, I want it known that I said a prayer first.”

At the end of the lane, in the dimness under a broken streetlight, Tejas sat astride his motorbike with his helmet on and his phone held against his chest like a rosary. He lifted one thumb. Ira lifted one back. It was absurdly like a film, and she was suddenly, fiercely glad to be inside it.

They went round the back, along a narrow gap between the wall and a stack of wooden crates that smelled of wet fish and cardboard. The shed was exactly where the pencilled note had said, a low annexe with a tin roof and a steel door that had been padlocked and then, at some stage, broken open and hung back on a loop of wire to look whole. It swung when Deepak touched it. Inside, the air was cold in a way that had nothing to do with ice. Ira swept her phone torch along the wall, and the light slid across rows and rows of curved blue metal, and she stopped breathing.

Drums. Dozens of them, stacked in ranks to the roof beams, blue steel, each with a paper label stuck on its side in black marker. ICE. DO NOT OPEN. A hundred and more, at least, standing in the dark like a congregation of sleeping animals. Deepak put his palm flat on the nearest one. He knocked on it twice with a knuckle. It rang like a bell, deep and full, and went on ringing a little after he took his hand away.
“Ice does not ring,” he said quietly.

He unscrewed the cap with a coin from his pocket and put his face over the opening and breathed in. She watched his expression change in the glow of her phone. It was not fear. It was something slower and angrier, the look of a man who has been told all his life that a certain thing could not be true. “Diesel,” he said. “Hundreds of litres of it. This is subsidised marine diesel, Ira. The blue-dyed kind, the kind that is only sold against a fisherman’s card to a boat with a registration number.” He screwed the cap back on, very carefully, and wiped his fingers on his jeans. “If you take it out of the harbour and sell it to a lorry company, you can get thirty rupees more a litre. If you do that with a hundred and fourteen imaginary boats’ worth of quota for three years…”
“Then you don’t need a boat at all,” said Ira. “Only a number.”

She was photographing the labels, one after the other, her hands very steady now that there was something to do, when she heard it. Outside, in the lane, a car door closed. Then another. The sound was soft, almost polite, and utterly unmistakable, the sound of people who know exactly where they are going and are in no hurry to get there.
Her phone buzzed against her palm. One word from Tejas, a single frantic message. CAR!!! TWO MEN!!!

Deepak was already moving, one hand on her sleeve, pulling her back between the drums. “Torch off,” he breathed. Ira thumbed the light out. The darkness closed over them like a hand. For a moment there was nothing at all except the thin high rushing sound of her own blood and the cold breath of diesel in her throat. Then they both heard the footsteps. Slow, heavy, deliberate, crossing the gravel towards the broken door, and with them the soft, patient, unhurried jingle of a bunch of keys.

episodes.title: Locked In
episodes.recap: At the old Sasi ice plant, Ira and Deepak find rows of barrels marked ICE that are full of subsidised diesel. Two men arrive outside with a bunch of keys.
text: The door closed with a sound like a dropped anvil. Light that she had not noticed was coming in through the gap, grey and thin, slid out of the shed like a held breath, and Ira found herself standing in complete darkness with her heart doing something drastic against her ribs. Outside, a key turned in a padlock and a chain rattled home. A voice said something in Tulu that she understood only by its tone, which was the tone of a man closing up a shop at the end of a long day. Another voice laughed. Then boots crunched away across the gravel and a car door closed, and a car started and went off, unhurried, down the lane.
“We are locked in,” said Deepak, from somewhere in the dark, in the calm voice of a man who is not calm.
“Yes.”
“In a shed. Full of illegal diesel.”
“Yes.”
“And I believe,” he said, as the first roll of thunder came over the estuary, “that it is about to rain.”

It did. It began on the tin roof like a handful of gravel thrown by a child, and then it came down in earnest, hammering, roaring, in a deluge so loud that Ira had to put her mouth to Deepak’s ear to be heard. Water found the gaps in the roof at once and began to drip, in cold, regular, mocking drops, onto the drums, which rang each in its own pitch, so that the whole shed sounded like a badly tuned orchestra. They tried the door and found it as solid as a cliff. They tried the one high window, a narrow oblong barred with iron. Deepak lifted her up and she got her fingers through the bars and saw only rain, the long white scribble of it in the light from a distant lamp, and the dark shape of the lorries beyond, not a soul anywhere.

He tried to ring his station and got a screen that said NO SERVICE. Ira tried to ring Mrs Kamath and got the same. It was the least helpful phone network in the history of India, Deepak remarked bitterly, and the only thing he had ever been grateful to it for was that it was entirely impartial about whom it abandoned. They sat down on two upturned crates with their backs against the cold curve of the drums, and for a long time neither said anything. Ira found that she was shaking, a little, from the cold and the wet and the adrenaline draining out of her like water from a basin. Deepak took off his cap, wrung it out and put it back on, and said conversationally, “If we die here, my mother will be very annoyed. She was planning to find me a wife this Diwali.”
“Mine too,” said Ira. “A chartered accountant.”
“Is he nice?”
“I have never met him.”

“Then he is probably nicer than either of us.” He laughed, a short, rueful bark in the dark, and she laughed too, and it was strange how much better the shed felt for it. “Ira,” he said, after a while, in an altogether different voice, “what you said at the tea stall, about the man who is hiding or being hidden. Do you think Mr Pinto knew this was here?”

“He wrote it on the cover. He knew.” She hugged her knees. “He wrote it down so that someone would come and find it, and then he went away so that no one would find him. It is the most cowardly brave thing I have ever heard of.”
“It is what most of us do,” said Deepak.

It was Ira who heard it first, under the roar of the rain. At first she thought it was part of the storm, a low, uneven, rattling sound underneath the thunder, like a heart with a cold. But it did not rise and fall as the wind did. It came on steadily, getting louder. It was an engine. Not a car’s engine, which purrs and hums, but an old engine, a worn and complaining one, the kind that coughs at every second stroke and has to be coaxed. She knew that sound. She had heard it in a boat yard, from underneath a hull, with a pair of cracked rubber sandals sticking out.
“Deepak,” she said. “Listen.”

The engine stopped, with a final cough, outside the door. Someone dropped something heavy on the gravel. There was a scrape of metal, a grunt, a long, ugly, grinding crack, and the chain fell off the door in two pieces. The door swung open, and the rain and the grey storm light came pouring in, and in the middle of it stood Yusuf Beary, soaked to the skin, with a crowbar over his shoulder and a cap pulled down over his eyes and, behind him, at the mouth of the lane, an auto-rickshaw with its engine still running and a very large boy in a helmet half out of the driver’s seat.

“Madam,” said Yusuf. “I told you to ask quietly.” He glanced at Deepak and at the barrels, and his broad face went through three or four expressions, none of them surprised. “Tejas telephoned me. He said the two of you were in the ice plant and two men had locked you in. I said, naturally. Now, quickly. Get in the auto. They will come back to look.”

They ran. The rain hit them like a wall. Tejas, white-faced with relief, was already shouting something about his hero’s welcome. Yusuf slammed the door of the shed, hung the broken chain back across it so that it looked exactly as it had before, and climbed in beside the driver, and the auto-rickshaw lurched off down the flooded lane with all four of them crushed into it like fish in a basket. Behind them the ice plant stood in the dark, tall and blind and silent. Ira looked back at it through the streaming plastic window and thought, with a clarity that surprised her, that she would never again be able to hear the word ice without hearing a bell.

episodes.title: Pinto Speaks
episodes.recap: Locked into the shed in a thunderstorm, Ira and Deepak are rescued by Yusuf Beary and Tejas, who arrive in an auto-rickshaw.
text: They did not sleep. Yusuf drove them in the auto-rickshaw to his boat yard, where his wife, a small, calm woman with a gold nose-stud and an air of having seen every kind of emergency, produced dry towels, a kettle and a plate of hot, soft bread without asking a single question. By two in the morning Deepak was asleep on a bench with his cap over his face and Tejas was telling the story of the rescue, for the fourth time, to an audience of one very patient cat. At half past four Ira slipped out into the grey wash of dawn, borrowed Yusuf’s second-best umbrella, and took the first bus north to Kundapura, because the only person who could tell her what the ledger meant was the man who had written it.

It had occurred to her somewhere around three o’clock, in the rattle and wheeze of the boat yard, that the old man’s sister lived in Kundapura. It was on the cooperative card, in the clerk’s small hand, under next of kin: Nirmala, sister, with an address on a lane behind the Panchagangavalli river. She had read it a dozen times and had not understood it until now. A man who was hiding does not go to a place where he has no one. He goes to the one door in the world that will be opened to him without a question.

The road to Kundapura ran for ninety kilometres along the coast, past rivers brimming and brown, past coconut groves with their crowns thrashing in the wind, past roadside shrines and school buses and long, low, tile-roofed houses with washing hung out in defiance of the rain. Ira sat at a window seat with her forehead against the glass, a damp rolled-up newspaper on her knee, and watched the country go by without seeing it. She was tired in a way she had not known existed. She was also, strangely, very clear. It was as if the night in the shed had burned something off her, and what was left was plain and hard and simple, like a stone at the bottom of a stream.

Nirmala Pinto’s house stood at the end of a lane of laterite walls and flowering bougainvillea, a low whitewashed cottage with a courtyard, a tulsi plant, a clothesline and a very large black dog named Sultan who lay across the doorstep like a rug. Sultan raised his head as Ira came through the gate, examined her shoes with extreme care for what felt like a full minute, and then, evidently satisfied, put his chin back on his paws and sighed. The door opened. A broad, grey-haired woman in a blue cotton sari, with floury forearms and a pair of spectacles on a string, looked at her and said, in a tone of neither surprise nor hostility, “You are the girl from the newspaper. He said you would come. He said you would be late, and that you would be wet.”

Mr Pinto was sitting at the kitchen table with a steel tumbler of tea in his hands, as if it might try to escape. He had grown thinner in four days. He wore a borrowed checked shirt that hung off his shoulders, and the stubble on his chin was white. When Ira came in he stood up, then sat down again, as if his knees had not made up their minds, and said, in a hoarse, careful voice, “You read it.”
“I read it,” said Ira. “And last night I nearly died in an ice plant because of it.”

He winced as though she had struck him. For a while he said nothing at all. Nirmala put a plate of hot idlis in front of Ira, with a bowl of coconut chutney, and stood with her arms folded against the stove, looking at her brother with a mixture of exasperation and love that Ira recognised from her own mother. “Then you know,” said Mr Pinto at last, “that I was right to run.”

“I know that you were frightened. I do not know yet whether you were right.” Ira sat down across from him. She had thought for ninety kilometres about what she would say, and what came out was nothing she had prepared. “Mr Pinto, why did you give it to me?”

He turned the tumbler round and round in his hands. The rain ticked on the tiles above them. A hen walked across the courtyard outside, stopped to consider the situation, and went on. “Miss Rao, I am not a hero,” he said at last. “I want you to understand that first, because I think you have been imagining that I am. I am a clerk. For thirty-one years I wrote what I was told to write and called it my job. When they began adding boats that did not exist, I told myself that it was accounting. That there were reasons I was not told. A clerk learns to say that, you know. That there are reasons. It is the most useful sentence in the language.”

He drank some tea. His hands shook. “It was in the third year. I came in early one morning, I had forgotten my spectacles, and I saw the diesel being loaded at the back, in the dark, onto a lorry that was not ours. There was no one else there. There were only the barrels, and a man in a white shirt standing and counting them with his lips, the way my father used to count coconuts. And I thought, that is what is behind column seven. It is not a boat. It is not a number. It is that man, counting, in the dark. And I understood that I had been writing it down for three years.”
“You wrote everything down.”

“That is what a clerk does when he is afraid. He writes things down.” He looked at her, and for the first time his eyes were steady. “The man’s name is Prabhakar. He works for Mr Hegde. He is not the dangerous one. He is only the one who is always there. And I heard him say to another man, last year, that the old book was ashes. That Pinto burned it himself, on the day he retired. I let him believe it. I let all of them believe it, for a year, so that they would stop looking.”
“Where is the old book?”

The silence stretched. Sultan sighed on the doorstep. Nirmala took the lid off a pot, looked into it, and put it back. “It is somewhere safe,” said Mr Pinto. “I will tell you where, Miss Rao, when you have given me one promise. When you have read it, you must read all of it. Not only the pages that are about them. All of it.” He put the tumbler down. “It says things about me, too. When you have read it, you may not want to protect me. I have not told you everything. I should like you to hear that from me, before you hear it from a page.”

episodes.title: The Scanner
episodes.recap: In Kundapura, Mr Pinto tells Ira why he kept the ledger and says an older book exists, hidden somewhere safe. He warns her that it also says things about him.
text: Ira did what every reporter must do before she does anything else, which is to make copies. There was a stationery shop near the Kundapura bus stand, a narrow, cluttered booth between a pharmacy and a shop selling plastic buckets, run by a man named Ganesh who owned one scanner, six hundred rubber stamps, and an unshakeable faith in the goodness of anyone who bought expensive envelopes. He sat behind a counter piled with pens, files, birthday cards and a small brass Ganesha with a marigold, and as Ira came in he put down the newspaper he was reading and looked at her ledger the way a doctor looks at a patient who has been in an accident.
“Ledger pages?” he said. “Two rupees a page. Three for the colour.”
“Black and white is fine.”

“Nobody wants the colour of an accounts book, Madam,” said Ganesh, with sorrow, and began to feed the pages one by one into the machine. It took a long time. The scanner hummed and clicked and slid a thin green light across each sheet, and every time it paused Ira found herself holding her breath. Deepak, who had come up on a later bus with his hair still wet and his expression still faintly affronted, stood at the door and watched the road. Tejas, who had insisted on bringing the motorbike all the way from Mangaluru through a drizzle that would have drowned a duck, sat on a stool eating a vada with great seriousness. And Sultan the dog, who had followed them from Nirmala’s lane for reasons of his own and had taken up a position under the counter, watched Ganesh’s samosa.

By four o’clock there were files on three memory cards, two email accounts and one very old laptop that belonged to Nirmala, and they all contained the same seventy pages of numbers. Ira had also had them printed. A full second copy sat in a brown envelope on the counter, heavy as a loaf. She put the first card inside her shoe, in the lining, under her left arch, where it made a small hard lump that she would feel for the next three days. The second she addressed in block capitals to Mrs Leela Kamath, The Coastal Courier, Hampankatta, with a note that said only In case, and put into the post box outside, where it vanished with a small wet sound. The third she gave to Deepak, who looked at it as if he had been handed a small, warm and slightly mutinous animal.
“What do I do with this?”
“Keep it. Do not use it. If I vanish, you use it.”
“That is not funny.”
“It is a little funny.”

“It is a little funny,” Deepak admitted, and put the card in his wallet, behind a photograph of his mother, where nobody would think to look. He was silent a moment. Then he said, with a rare, grave courtesy, “Ira, I have not told you something. When I rang my station this morning, my senior officer was in a strange mood. He asked why I was in Kundapura on a day off. I did not tell him I was in Kundapura. I told him I was at home.”
She looked at him.
“He asked,” said Deepak, “because someone had told him.”

The air in the little shop seemed to cool. Outside, a bus ground away from the stand with a gasp of brakes. A girl went by on a bicycle with a bouquet of wet marigolds in her basket. It was, Ira thought, the oddest thing about danger: that it arrived dressed as an ordinary Monday, with the vendors still calling, and a child still crying for an ice-cream, and the sky an everyday colourless grey. “Who knew?” she said.
“That is what I am afraid of,” said Deepak. “Nobody. Nobody knew. Which is the same as everybody.”

They were about to leave when Ira’s phone rang. It was the newsroom number. She thought it would be Mrs Kamath, with some question about the pothole page, or about the second source, and she answered with her heart already starting its slow, tired climb. But it was not Mrs Kamath. It was Sheshappa, the old peon, who had never before in eleven months telephoned her, and who spoke now in a whisper, in a rapid Kannada that she had to listen to twice. He said that he was calling from the back stairs. He said that a car had arrived at the front of the building half an hour ago. He said that it was a long grey Innova, with a driver, and that a gentleman had got out of the back with a lawyer, and that the lawyer was carrying a briefcase and a long stamped paper.
“Madam,” said Sheshappa, his voice cracking. “He is at the Courier. Mr Hegde is in the office. He has gone in to see Madam Kamath. And Madam,” he added, “he is smiling.”

episodes.title: Deadline
episodes.recap: Ira has the ledger scanned in Kundapura, then learns that Mr Hegde is at the newsroom with a lawyer and a court paper.
text: By the time Ira reached the newsroom the sun had set and the rain had come back, apologising. She had taken a bus and then a taxi, and then, at the Pumpwell flyover where the traffic had come to a standstill, got out and run, with the brown envelope under her shirt and Tejas pounding after her, his camera bags slapping against his hips. She took the stairs two at a time. The lights were on in Mrs Kamath’s glass office, and through the glass she could see three people. One was the editor, upright, hands folded on her blotter. One was a nervous man in a black coat holding a briefcase on his knees as if it might be taken from him. And one, in the visitor’s chair, with his ankles crossed, at his ease, with a cup of tea in front of him that someone had brought on a saucer, was R K Hegde.

He was not smiling. That was the worst of it. Sheshappa had been wrong, or the smile had been put away as she came in. Without the smile, with the lamp behind him lighting the silver of his hair, he looked like a man who owned a large quiet piece of the sea, and had never doubted for a moment that he would go on owning it.
Mrs Kamath opened the door herself. “Ira,” she said. “Come in. Mr Hegde has been kind enough to bring us something.”

The lawyer cleared his throat. He was a young man, perhaps thirty-five, with a thin nervous moustache and a voice that kept starting a little too high. He drew a long, stamped sheet from his briefcase and laid it on the blotter, and smoothed it flat with both palms. It was printed in English, in small type, on legal paper that bore the seal of the District Court. Ira read the first lines without touching it. The Honourable Court has been pleased to grant an interim order restraining The Coastal Courier, its editors, reporters and agents, from publishing, printing or circulating, whether in print, online or otherwise, any statement concerning the affairs, accounts, directors or transactions of Sea Crest Marine Private Limited or its chairman, pending further orders.
“It was granted this afternoon,” said the lawyer, in a high voice. “At three-twenty. You have all been served.”
Ira looked at the paper, and then at Mr Hegde. “You knew what I was going to write,” she said, “before I had written it.”

“I know a great many things, Miss Rao,” said Mr Hegde, very gently. He lifted the cup, set it down again, and she saw that his hand was perfectly steady. “For instance, I know that a story printed in a hurry can ruin an honest man. I have seen it happen. I have a friend in Bengaluru who lost a school, and a daughter’s wedding, to a headline that was corrected on page seven.” He folded his hands. “You are young, and bright, and you have the courage that I should like to see in all the young people of this coast. It would be a great pity for you to make a mistake that cannot be put right. I came myself, Mrs Kamath, because I did not wish to send a letter. Letters are unkind. I wished to say it in person: I am not your enemy. I have only ever wished to protect what we have built together on this coast.”

Mrs Kamath did not move. She sat with her eyes on the injunction, reading it, or pretending to, for a long time. The ceiling fan turned. Out in the newsroom, someone had stopped typing and the silence of fifty people pretending not to listen pressed on the glass like a hand. When she raised her head Ira could not read her face at all. It was the face of a woman at the edge of a very high place, with her eyes on something very far away. She did not look at Ira. She looked at Mr Hegde. And then, slowly, and for the first time in the eleven years that Ira had known her, she took off her glasses and laid them on the desk, which was, as everyone in the building knew, the thing she did immediately before she made a decision that she would not take back.

“Thank you for coming, Mr Hegde,” said Mrs Kamath. “And you, sir,” she added, to the lawyer, who flinched. “I shall read this with care and I shall consult our own counsel. If you will be kind enough to leave us.”

The two men stood. Mr Hegde bowed slightly, a gracious, courtly bow, and moved to the door, and as he passed Ira he paused, just for a moment. He did not look at her. He looked, a little to one side, at the brown envelope that had made a faint square outline under her shirt. Then he smiled again, the old smile, warm as the lunch table, and went out through the newsroom, between the silent desks, to the stairs.

The door closed. A fan turned. For a long moment no one in the glass room spoke. Then Mrs Kamath put her spectacles back on, folded her hands, and said, quietly, in a voice that carried to every corner of the room, “Everyone, please leave this office. Except Ira.”
